1	# CS370 Term Project — Team Rules
2	
3	**Project:** `carwatch` — an always-on in-vehicle diagnostic recorder that learns *this*
4	car's normal and reports developing faults before a check-engine light would.
5	
6	**Team:** Camden Thomas (`crash8750@gmail.com`) · Lance Baron
7	**Course:** CS 370 Operating Systems, Colorado State University (Pallickara)
8	**Handout:** `CS370-TermProject.pdf` v1.0 (2026-08-03) — the rubric is law; this file is
9	how we obey it.
10	
11	> **Read this file every session.** It is team law, maintained by both partners. A
12	> constraint that lives only in one partner's head protects nothing.
13	
14	---
15	
16	## 0. How to use this file
17	
18	You (Claude) are required in our **workflow** and forbidden in our **product**
19	(handout §3.3, §10.3). Every session, in this order:
20	
21	1. Read this file.
22	2. Read `docs/milestones.md` — where we are and what the exit criteria are.
23	3. Read `docs/DECISIONS.md` — what is already settled, and what is awaiting review.
24	4. Read `docs/BOARD.md`, then run `python tools/board_sync.py --status` — what is Ready,
25	   what is holding up the critical path, and how long each open question has been open.
26	5. State whose session this is. Do not edit outside that owner's area without being told.
27	6. `git status` must be clean. Create the branch **before** the first edit.
28	
29	Do not reopen a decision marked 🔒 LOCKED without saying so explicitly and getting a
30	human yes.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 1. Commands
35	
36	```
37	make              # build everything, -Wall -Wextra -Werror clean
38	make test         # unit tests + the boundary check
39	make asan         # build+run tests under AddressSanitizer + UBSan
40	make memcheck     # valgrind over the test binaries
41	make soakcheck    # 1-hour miniature of the 48h run
42	make hwcheck      # KiCad ERC; violations fail the build, like -Werror
43	make hwdocs       # regenerate schematic SVG, BOM and netlist from the schematic
44	make replay FIX=fixtures/<name>   # run a labeled capture through the real pipeline
45	make deploy PI=pi@<host>          # rsync + remote build
46	make clean
47	
48	python tools/board_sync.py --status    # what is Ready, what is stuck, who owns it
49	python tools/board_sync.py --check     # has the board drifted? (exit 1 if yes)
50	python tools/board_sync.py             # reconcile docs/board.toml onto GitHub
51	```
52	
53	**A change is DONE only when `make`, `make test`, and `make asan` all pass, and you have
54	shown me the output.** Not "should pass." Output, pasted.
55	
56	---
57	
58	## 2. Hard constraints — these are graded boundaries
59	
60	1. **No hosted models in the product.** No LLM API calls, no cloud inference, no network
61	   calls of any kind except serving its own LAN interface. A grader must confirm this in
62	   sixty seconds by reading the tree. `src/` contains no HTTP client. Ever.
63	2. **Our model, our weights.** Classifier trained by us, on our data, training code in
64	   `tools/train/`, weights versioned in `models/`. No third-party pretrained weights.
65	   Inference is C we wrote.
66	3. **The device works with the network unplugged.** Full stop.
67	4. **Systems core is C17**, `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, no VLAs, `goto`-cleanup for
68	   multi-resource functions. Every allocation checked. Every syscall error path handled
69	   *and logged*.
70	5. **Python lives only in `tools/` and `ui/`.** No graded mechanism may hide there.
71	6. **Every daemon is supervisable:** clean exit codes, no orphaned fds across restart,
72	   heartbeat within 60 s of start, survives `kill -9` of any sibling.
73	7. **Replayed or synthesized data is labeled as such EVERYWHERE** — every record carries
74	   `src=live|replay|synth`. Integrity boundary, not a style choice.
75	8. **Never weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass.** If a test is wrong,
76	   say so and fix it deliberately, in its own commit, with the reason.
77	
78	---
79	
80	## 3. What we are building (the one-paragraph version)
81	
82	A Raspberry Pi riding in a daily-driven car. A USB OBD2 adapter in the car's OBD2 port
83	gives it the car's own sensors (D-015); the car's USB-C port powers it — nothing is cut or
84	spliced (D-011). Through standard Mode 01 requests (D-012) it reads oil temperature,
85	coolant temp, MAP, O2 / fuel trims, RPM and load, and builds a statistical model of what
86	normal looks like *for this car, at this operating point*. It then reports deviations
87	that a mileage sticker and a check-engine light both miss. The owner reads it from their
88	phone over the device's own Wi-Fi — read-only, no internet (D-013); `obdctl` stays the
89	exact interface. A single warning light on the box blinks while it is on duty and
90	changes pattern when something needs attention (D-014).
91	
92	**The user:** a named owner of a specific car who wants maintenance driven by measured
93	condition instead of a generic interval. Testbed: **Lance's 2015 Honda CR-V EX-L**, the
94	only one (D-016). Its sticker and its Maintenance Minder both *estimate* from how far and
95	how hard it has been driven; the device *measures* the engine's condition (D-007).
96	
97	**The claim we defend:** *"detects the three faults we can induce on this vehicle, with
98	these measured error rates."* Not "predicts failure." (handout §5)
99	
100	---
101	
102	## 4. Mechanism commitments
103	
104	We need two. We commit to **D** (append-only crash-consistent storage — power is cut at
105	every key-off) and **E** (multi-process with a supervisor), and measure both. **B**
106	(interrupt-driven input vs polling) and **F** (high-rate no-drop ring) come back only if a
107	Pi-side sensor is added (board item `pisensor`): Mode 01 through a USB adapter is too slow,
108	and has no interrupt of ours, to justify either. **A**, **C** and raw CAN are stretch only.
109	Full rationale: `docs/DECISIONS.md` §B.1 (D-017).
110	
111	---
112	
113	## 5. The intelligence
114	
115	All of it ours. Operating-point binning → per-bin baselines → Mahalanobis residuals →
116	Theil–Sen trends → our classifier → state machine with hysteresis. Rationale and the
117	standing "threshold test" rule: `docs/DECISIONS.md` §D.
118	
119	---
120	
121	## 6. Ownership map
122	
123	| Owner | Subsystems |
124	|---|---|
125	| **Camden** | `src/obd/`, `src/ipc/` |
126	| **Lance** | `src/store/`, `src/analysis/`, `tools/train/`, **`electricalDrawing/`** |
127	| **Shared** | `src/supervisor/`, `src/interface/`, `src/common/`, `Makefile`, docs |
128	
129	Ownership means first authorship and answerability at the defense, not exclusivity.
130	
131	---
132	
133	# 7. Git and pull-request law
134	
135	**This section is not advisory.** Our process grade is computed from transcripts
136	corroborated against commits; the git history is itself a graded deliverable; and neither
137	partner will break down a thousand-line diff to review it. A commit small enough to review
138	in ninety seconds is a commit that actually gets reviewed.
139	
140	## 7.1 The five absolutes
141	
142	Claude may **never**, under any instruction short of an explicit human override in the
143	current session:
144	
145	1. **Commit to `main`.** Every change reaches `main` through a pull request.
146	2. **Merge, approve, or close a pull request.** Only a human merges. Ever.
147	3. **`push --force`, force-with-lease, rebase a pushed branch, amend a pushed commit, or
148	   `reset --hard` anything that has been pushed.** History that reviewers have read is
149	   immutable.
150	4. **`git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`.** Stage explicit paths, always. An
151	   unintended file in a diff destroys a reviewer's trust in the whole PR.
152	5. **Commit a file whose full current contents were not read this session.** No blind
153	   edits to code you have not looked at.
154	
155	Violating any of these is a stop-work event: say so, and do not attempt a workaround.
156	
157	## 7.2 Branches
158	
159	- `main` is protected, always green, and never committed to directly.
160	- **One branch per unit of work.** Naming: `<owner>/<milestone>/<slug>`
161	  — `camden/m3/obd-reader`, `lance/m3/store-recovery`, `camden/m2/design-doc`.
162	- **A branch has exactly one purpose.** If you discover unrelated work mid-branch, you do
163	  not fold it in. Note it, finish the branch, open a separate one.
164	- Branch lifetime: one session's work, three days maximum. A long-lived branch is a
165	  review you will never do.
166	- Branch from current `main`, freshly pulled. Never branch from another open branch
167	  without saying so in the PR.
168	
169	## 7.3 Commit granularity — one commit, one responsibility
170	
171	**There is no line-count limit.** A commit is sized by *what it is responsible for*, not by
172	how big the diff happens to be. A 200-line rewrite of a single function is **one** commit;
173	splitting it would force the reviewer to hold half a function in their head across two
174	reviews, which is worse than the problem it solves. Twenty lines spread across five
175	unrelated concerns is **five** commits, even though it is small.
176	
177	**The test that decides it, every time:**
178	
179	> Can the reviewer evaluate this as a **single yes-or-no decision**?
180	
181	If approving requires accepting one part while objecting to another, it is more than one
182	commit. If rejecting any part means rejecting the whole thing anyway, it is one commit —
183	leave it alone.
184	
185	**The one-sentence test, restated.** State the commit's responsibility in one sentence
186	without using "and". If you can, it is one commit no matter how many lines it took. If you
187	cannot, split along the "and".
188	
189	### For code
190	
191	The unit is **one behavior, one function, or one design principle applied.**
192	
193	- Tests ship **in the same commit** as the behavior they test. Same responsibility.
194	- A refactor is its own responsibility — never folded into a feature.
195	- Formatting, renames, and file moves are **separate commits, labeled as such**, so the
196	  reviewer skims them at speed instead of hunting for logic buried in noise.
197	- Two subsystems means two commits, always, regardless of size.
198	- **Every commit builds and passes tests on its own.** This is the one hard rule in this
199	  section — it is what makes the history bisectable and each commit reviewable in isolation.
200	
201	**Size as a smell, not a limit.** Past roughly 400 changed lines, stop and re-apply the
202	one-sentence test — large diffs *often* contain a smuggled second responsibility. If it
203	survives the test, commit it as one unit and **say in the `WHY` why it is indivisible.**
204	Then the reviewer knows the size was considered rather than accidental.
205	
206	### For documentation, Markdown, and data files
207	
208	The unit is **one resolved question or one decision** — not one file, not one section.
209	
210	- Closing one open question that touches a line in six tables across three files is **one
211	  commit.** Splitting it is actively harmful: the reviewer can no longer see that the
212	  change was applied *consistently*, which is the only thing worth checking.
213	- A doc commit's diff is often wide and shallow. That is expected and correct.
214	- Never mix a **content** change with a **reflow/reformat** of the same file — the content
215	  change disappears into whitespace noise. Reformat separately, or not at all.
216	- Never mix filling in a TODO with restructuring the section around it.
217	- Never mix a decision's *record* with its *implementation* across files in a way that
218	  hides one inside the other — but **do** keep a decision and the code that enacts it
219	  together when they are genuinely one change (see §7.7).
220	
221	**The check:** `git show <commit>` should answer exactly one question a human asked. If it
222	answers two, split. If it answers half of one, you committed too early.
223	
224	## 7.4 Commit message format
225	
226	```
227	M<n> <area>: <imperative summary, ≤ 72 chars>
228	
229	WHAT:   One sentence. What changed, mechanically.
230	WHY:    1–3 sentences. The reason, in terms of a requirement, a decision ID,
231	        or a measurement. Never "to improve things."
232	REVIEW: What the reviewer should check hardest, and what I am least sure about.
233	VERIFY: The exact commands run and their result.
234	```
235	
236	`<area>` is one of: `obd`, `ipc`, `store`, `analysis`, `supervisor`,
237	`interface`, `common`, `build`, `tests`, `tools`, `soak`, `docs`.
238	
239	Real example:
240	
241	```
242	M3 ipc: refuse push on full ring instead of overwriting
243	
244	WHAT:   ring_push now returns false and increments an overrun counter when
245	        head - tail == RING_CAPACITY, rather than wrapping over slot[tail].
246	WHY:    DECISIONS.md B.3 — silent overwrite is the exact failure mechanism F
247	        exists to prevent; a gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis.
248	REVIEW: The memory ordering on the tail load. I used acquire so the producer
249	        cannot see a stale tail and wrongly declare the ring full; I am least
250	        sure whether relaxed would be sufficient here.
251	VERIFY: make && make test && make asan — all green, test_ring 3/3.
252	```
253	
254	**Banned messages**, non-negotiable: `wip`, `fix`, `fixes`, `updates`, `misc`, `cleanup`,
255	`changes`, `more work`, `address feedback`, or any message that does not say what changed.
256	
257	## 7.5 Pull requests
258	
259	- **One PR = one reviewable claim.** Title matches the lead commit: `M<n> <area>: <what>`.
260	- **A PR is sized by its claim, not its diff.** If the title needs "and", split it. If a
261	  reviewer would have to approve part and object to part, split it. A PR that implements
262	  one coherent thing is the right size even when that thing was large — but say so in the
263	  body, and lay out the commit-by-commit list so the reviewer has a path through it.
264	- **Past ~10 commits or ~600 changed lines, re-apply the test rather than obey a number.**
265	  Most PRs that big contain two claims; the ones that genuinely do not are fine.
266	- **Open the PR as a draft at the first commit**, not at the end — so the partner can watch
267	  it grow and object early instead of at the finish line.
268	- A PR touching the **other partner's** owned area is titled `[cross]` and needs that
269	  partner's review specifically, not either partner's.
270	- The description uses `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, **every section filled**. A PR
271	  with an unfilled section is not ready for review, and Claude should not mark it ready.
272	- The description must contain **verbatim pasted output** of `make`, `make test`, and
273	  `make asan`. Not a claim that they passed. The output.
274	- The description must name the decision IDs the PR touches, and must contain a
275	  **"What I am least sure about"** paragraph that is not empty. If everything is certain,
276	  you have not thought hard enough about the diff.
277	- If a PR needs a diagram, an annotated log excerpt, or a timing capture to be
278	  understandable — put it in the PR body. Making the reviewer reconstruct context is how
279	  reviews stop happening.
280	
281	## 7.6 The merge gate
282	
283	**If the reviewer does not understand a line, the pull request does not merge.**
284	
285	The remedy is never "trust it." The remedy is, in order of preference:
286	
287	1. Claude explains it in a PR comment, in plain language, tied to the requirement.
288	2. The commit is split further, so each piece is obvious on its own.
289	3. The code is rewritten more simply, even at a cost in elegance or a few instructions.
290	
291	A reviewer must be able to answer these about **any line** in the diff before approving —
292	they are the demo-day question set, asked early:
293	
294	- What wakes this? What is it waiting on?
295	- What happens to this file descriptor / this allocation when the child dies?
296	- What is the error path, and what does it log?
297	- Why can't this drop, duplicate, or reorder a sample?
298	- Which requirement or decision made it this way rather than the obvious alternative?
299	
300	Neither partner approves a PR they could not defend at the keyboard, alone, on demo day.
301	**Approving code you do not understand is the only unrecoverable mistake in this
302	workflow** — it is 20 individual points, and the defense will find it.
303	
304	## 7.7 Session start and session end
305	
306	**Start of session:**
307	1. Read `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/milestones.md`, `docs/DECISIONS.md`.
308	2. `python tools/board_sync.py --status` — pick work from **Ready**, nowhere else.
309	3. State whose session this is.
310	4. `git status` clean, `git pull` on `main`, create the branch.
311	
312	**End of session — mandatory, every time:**
313	1. Nothing uncommitted. No stray files.
314	2. PR opened or updated, template filled, build/test/asan output pasted.
315	3. **Every decision made without a human present is appended to `docs/DECISIONS.md` as
316	   ⚠️ UNREVIEWED and listed in the Review Queue — in the same commit that implements it,
317	   never a later one.**
318	4. Print a session summary: branch name, each commit as one line, PR link, decisions added,
319	   and what specifically needs human review.
320	
321	**Claude never marks a decision reviewed or LOCKED.** Only Camden or Lance does, by editing
322	the `Reviewed` field, in a commit authored by that human.
323	
324	## 7.8 When to stop instead of commit
325	
326	Stop and emit a structured blocker — the decision, the options, the cost of each, your
327	recommendation — rather than proceeding, when:
328	
329	- the change carries two responsibilities and cannot be cleanly separated (§7.3)
330	- it requires a decision not already in `docs/DECISIONS.md`
331	- it would touch the other partner's owned area by more than a line
332	- it would weaken, skip, or delete a test
333	- `make`, `make test`, or `make asan` is not green
334	- you would have to guess at hardware behavior without evidence (see §8)
335	
336	## 7.9 Volume and distribution
337	
338	≥ 40 meaningful commits across the semester, **both partners well represented**. A history
339	where one partner authored under a quarter of the substantive commits is probed hard at the
340	individual defense. A pair of "final submission" commits is an automatic process-grade of
341	zero **for both partners**.
342	
343	Commit *as you go*, inside the session. A session that produces one commit at the end has
344	already lost the granularity this section exists to protect.
345	
346	## 7.10 Repository settings (humans, once)
347	
348	On GitHub, set on `main`: require a pull request before merging · require 1 approval ·
349	dismiss stale approvals on new commits · require conversation resolution · block force
350	pushes · block deletions. Enable **squash-merge only if** the squash message is rewritten
351	to be meaningful — otherwise prefer merge commits, since our granular history *is* the
352	deliverable and squashing destroys it.
353	
354	## 7.11 Issues and the project board — where work and questions live
355	
356	**GitHub Issues replace the blockers list.** Anything that needs a human — a question, a
357	decision, a measurement only one of us can take, a part that must be ordered — is an
358	**issue**, not a paragraph buried in a doc or a session summary nobody re-reads.
359	
360	`docs/DECISIONS.md` keeps only what has been **decided** (plus the review queue).
361	Everything still open lives on the board, where it has an owner, a milestone, and a
362	visible position in the queue.
363	
364	### The board is generated, not hand-maintained
365	
366	**`docs/board.toml` is the source of truth. GitHub is derived from it.**
367	`tools/board_sync.py` reconciles the two. Full contract in `docs/BOARD.md`; the part that
368	binds this section:
369	
370	> **Never create, retitle, relabel, re-milestone or re-assign an issue with `gh` or in
371	> the web UI.** Edit the `[[item]]` and re-run sync. An issue created by hand is invisible
372	> to the manifest, drifts immediately, and is reported forever as unmanaged.
373	
374	What you *may* do directly on GitHub: **comment**, **answer**, and **close**. Those are the
375	human parts, and sync respects all three — it never reopens what a human closed, and it
376	reports any issue closed on GitHub that `board.toml` still thinks is open, so the manifest
377	gets caught up in the next commit.
378	
379	### Issue types
380	
381	| Label | Meaning | Who closes it |
382	|---|---|---|
383	| `question` | Needs human judgment or knowledge Claude does not have | **Human only** |
384	| `decision` | A design choice that must be made before work proceeds | **Human only** |
385	| `task` | Work to be done; may be Claude's or a human's | PR merge, or owner |
386	| `bug` | Something is wrong | PR merge |
387	| `hardware` | Physical world: order it, wire it, measure it, drive it | **Human only** |
388	| `blocked` | Waiting on a dependency (applied and removed by sync) | n/a |
389	
390	`board_sync.py` refuses to close a `question`, `decision` or `hardware` issue without the
391	explicit `--close-questions` flag, which is a human typing it. That is the enforcement, not
392	an honour system.
393	
394	### Claude's standing instructions
395	
396	- **When you would stop and emit a blocker (§7.8), add an `[[item]]` to `docs/board.toml`
397	  instead**, run sync, and continue with whatever else is unblocked. Link the issue number
398	  in the session summary.
399	- Title: `M<n> <area>: <what>` — same convention as commits.
400	- Body must state: what is blocked, what you already tried or know, the options with their
401	  costs, your recommendation, and **exactly what answer would unblock it**. A question a
402	  human can answer in one line beats a question that needs a meeting.
403	- Set `owner`. Unassigned issues are nobody's.
404	- Set `milestone` (`M0`–`M6`) so the board sorts by deadline.
405	- Give it a `slug` that will still make sense in Week 14. Slugs are permanent identity —
406	  **never rename or reuse one**; the slug→issue mapping in `docs/board.lock.json` is what
407	  survives between sessions.
408	- If the item exists because of a decision, set `decision = "D-###"`. Sync renders the link
409	  into the issue and warns if that ID is not in `docs/DECISIONS.md`.
410	
411	### Dependencies — the gate
412	
413	`blocked_by` in `board.toml` takes **slugs, never issue numbers**. Sync resolves them,
414	writes the `Blocked by: #12, #15` block into the body, and applies or removes the `blocked`
415	label as blockers open and close. It refuses to run on a dependency cycle or a dangling
416	slug, so a bad edit fails before it reaches GitHub.
417	
418	The board column follows from that, automatically:
419	
420	| Column | Means |
421	|---|---|
422	| **Backlog** | something it depends on is still open |
423	| **Ready** | nothing blocks it — this is the actionable list |
424	| **Blocked** | waiting on something that is *not* another item (a shipment, a reply) — set by hand |
425	| **In progress** / **In review** | set by hand while work is live |
426	| **Done** | the issue is closed |
427	
428	**Do not start work on an issue that is not in Ready** — say so and pick up something that
429	is. Answering one question can move several cards into Ready on the next sync; that is the
430	board telling you what just became workable.
431	
432	### Issue → branch → PR, as one chain
433	
434	```sh
435	gh issue develop <n> --name camden/m3/obd-reader --checkout   # branch linked to issue
436	# ... commits per §7.3 ...
437	gh pr create --draft --title "M3 obd: Mode 01 reader on the adapter tty" --body-file <filled template>
438	```
439	
440	The PR body must contain `Closes #<n>`. Merging then closes the issue; the next sync moves
441	the card to Done. **Every PR traces back to an issue**; if there is no issue, add the
442	`[[item]]` first — that is the record of *why* the work existed.
443	
444	### Session end
445	
446	Run `python tools/board_sync.py`. It is the only thing that moves cards, and it is cheap:
447	a run with nothing to do makes zero writes. **A board that lies is worse than no board**,
448	and the only way it can lie now is if you skipped this step.
449	
450	CI enforces it: `.github/workflows/board.yml` runs `--check --no-board` on every push and
451	pull request and fails on drift, and `make test` validates `docs/board.toml` itself through
452	`tools/test_board.py`. So a forgotten sync is a red build, not a quiet lie.
453	
454	### What this is worth at the defense
455	
456	The board is not project-management theater. It is a timestamped record that the questions
457	were asked before the work, that a human answered them, and that the answer shaped the
458	code — which is precisely the process the transcripts are graded against, corroborated by
459	an independent system we did not write.
460	
461	---
462	
463	## 7.12 Hardware changes (KiCad)
464	
465	The schematic lives in `electricalDrawing/` (KiCad 10, owned by Lance). KiCad files are
466	S-expression **text**, so hardware goes through the same branches, commits and pull requests
467	as the C — with two additions, both of which exist because a reviewer cannot read a diff of
468	coordinate tuples.
469	
470	**Every PR touching `electricalDrawing/` must:**
471	
472	1. **Include the regenerated schematic SVG** (`make hwdocs`, commit
473	   `docs/figures/electricalDrawing.svg`). A hardware PR without a picture is unreviewable,
474	   and §7.6 then blocks it — correctly.
475	2. **Show `make hwcheck` output in the body.** ERC violations are build failures, the same
476	   way `-Werror` findings are. Pasted output, not a claim.
477	
478	**Commit granularity for schematics** follows the documentation rule in §7.3, not the code
479	rule: the unit is **one functional block or one resolved electrical question**. Wiring the
480	whole CAN block is one commit even if it moves fifty symbols. Renumbering references across
481	the sheet is a separate, labeled commit — never folded into a wiring change, for exactly the
482	reason formatting is never folded into logic.
483	
484	**Never commit:** `.kicad_prl` (per-user state), `.history/`, autosave or backup files, or
485	anything under `make hwdocs`'s outputs except the schematic SVG. The `.gitignore` enforces
486	this.
487	
488	**What Claude may not do here.** I cannot see the board. Symbol pin numbering, footprint
489	choice, placement, thermal, EMI and mechanical fit are all things I reason about blind, and
490	hand-writing `.kicad_pcb` geometry is forbidden — the coordinate math fails silently at fab.
491	I am useful for netlist review, datasheet cross-checks, design rules, BOM and export
492	scripting, and reading ERC JSON. **A measured voltage always beats my opinion**, and §8.4
493	applies with full force: no hardware conclusion from a verbal description or an unmeasured
494	module.
495	
496	---
497	
498	---
499	
500	## 8. Workflow (non-git)
501	
502	1. **Plan first.** Multi-file or algorithmic change: plan mode, wait for approval, no code
503	   until the plan is accepted.
504	2. **Explore before writing.** Read the existing code and the datasheet before proposing.
505	   Say what you read.
506	3. **Tests lead.** New behavior gets a test that fails first.
507	4. **Evidence over assertion — hardware clause (handout §10.2).** Never propose a hardware
508	   fix from a verbal description. Paste the artifact: `dmesg` verbatim, the raw adapter
509	   replies, the `vcgencmd get_throttled` reading, the timing histogram.
510	   Without evidence, your job is to say what to capture — not to guess.
511	5. **Adversarial review.** Every milestone's diff gets a fresh-context agent review *and* a
512	   human review by the partner who did not write it.
513	6. **Smallest diff that passes.** Do not refactor unrelated code. Do not "improve" things
514	   nobody asked about.
515	7. **Autonomous execution with declared blockers.** Run to completion on everything you
516	   can; stop with structured output at decisions that need human judgment.
517	8. **Credit discipline.** Minimal tool calls, no re-reads of files already in context, no
518	   re-derivation of settled results, batch independent work, smallest edits.
519	
520	### Prompt quality bar (handout §10.4)
521	
522	Useless: "make the sensor work." Effective: "`/dev/obd` opens and `ATZ` answers, but
523	`010C` returns `NO DATA` with the engine running. Here is our init sequence and the raw
524	replies [paste both]. Diff them against the ELM327 datasheet's protocol-selection steps and
525	identify the missing one; do not rewrite the reader."
526	
527	---
528	
529	## 9. Milestone hygiene — do not let this slip
530	
531	**At every milestone M1–M5, each partner copies their raw `.jsonl` session files out of
532	`~/.claude/projects/` into `partners/<name>/transcripts/`.** Raw. Not summarized, not
533	exported, not retyped. Transcripts purge after 30 days by default and this project runs 15
534	weeks — losing Week-5 transcripts in Week 15 is a *foreseeable* loss and is not excused.
535	
536	Each partner maintains `partners/<name>/PROMPTLOG.md` — 6–10 annotated episodes by M5,
537	including one revised plan, one rejected diff, one tool-output debugging loop with real
538	hardware evidence, and one review of the partner's work. **Write these as they happen.**
539	
540	---
541	
542	## 10. Deliverables checklist (handout §12)
543	
544	- [ ] Source + `Makefile` + `README.md` that takes a TA from a clean Pi to running
545	- [ ] `docs/PROBLEM.md` (as revised), `docs/DESIGN.md` (as it ended + changelog of what M2 got
546	      wrong), `docs/EVALUATION.md`
547	- [ ] Raw unedited 48-hour soak logs including the injected fault
548	- [ ] `CLAUDE.md`, checked in, visibly evolving across milestones
549	- [ ] Per partner: `PROMPTLOG.md`, `REFLECTION.md`, raw `.jsonl` transcripts
550	- [ ] ≥ 40 meaningful commits spanning the milestones, both partners represented
551	
552	---
553	
554	## 11. Open blockers
555	
556	**On the board, not in this file.** Open `question` and `decision` issues, in the Backlog
557	column of the `carwatch` project. `python tools/board_sync.py --status` lists them with
558	how long each has been open.
559	`docs/DECISIONS.md` records only what has been *decided*, plus the review queue. Nothing
560	open is tracked in two places, so nothing open can go stale in one of them.
561	
562	---
563	
564	*Last updated: M0 — §0, §7.11 and §11 rewritten when the board moved to
565	`docs/board.toml` + `tools/board_sync.py`. Both partners maintain this file.*
566

# CS370 Term Project — Team Rules

**Project:** `carwatch` — an always-on in-vehicle diagnostic recorder that learns *this*
car's normal and reports developing faults before a check-engine light would.

**Team:** Camden Thomas (`crash8750@gmail.com`) · Lance Baron
**Course:** CS 370 Operating Systems, Colorado State University (Pallickara)
**Handout:** `CS370-TermProject.pdf` v1.0 (2026-08-03) — the rubric is law; this file is
how we obey it.

> **Read this file every session.** It is team law, maintained by both partners. A
> constraint that lives only in one partner's head protects nothing.

---

## 0. How to use this file

You (Claude) are required in our **workflow** and forbidden in our **product**
(handout §3.3, §10.3). Every session, in this order:

1. Read this file.
2. Read `docs/milestones.md` — where we are and what the exit criteria are.
3. Read `docs/DECISIONS.md` — what is already settled, and what is awaiting review.
4. Read `docs/BOARD.md`, then run `python tools/board_sync.py --status` — what is Ready,
   what is holding up the critical path, and how long each open question has been open.
5. State whose session this is. Do not edit outside that owner's area without being told.
6. `git status` must be clean. Create the branch **before** the first edit.

Do not reopen a decision marked 🔒 LOCKED without saying so explicitly and getting a
human yes.

---

## 1. Commands

```
make              # build everything, -Wall -Wextra -Werror clean
make test         # unit tests + the boundary check
make asan         # build+run tests under AddressSanitizer + UBSan
make memcheck     # valgrind over the test binaries
make soakcheck    # 1-hour miniature of the 48h run
make hwcheck      # KiCad ERC; violations fail the build, like -Werror
make hwdocs       # regenerate schematic SVG, BOM and netlist from the schematic
make replay FIX=fixtures/<name>   # run a labeled capture through the real pipeline
make deploy PI=pi@<host>          # rsync + remote build
make clean

python tools/board_sync.py --status    # what is Ready, what is stuck, who owns it
python tools/board_sync.py --check     # has the board drifted? (exit 1 if yes)
python tools/board_sync.py             # reconcile docs/board.toml onto GitHub
```

**A change is DONE only when `make`, `make test`, and `make asan` all pass, and you have
shown me the output.** Not "should pass." Output, pasted.

---

## 2. Hard constraints — these are graded boundaries

1. **No hosted models in the product.** No LLM API calls, no cloud inference, no network
   calls of any kind except serving its own LAN interface. A grader must confirm this in
   sixty seconds by reading the tree. `src/` contains no HTTP client. Ever.
2. **Our model, our weights.** Classifier trained by us, on our data, training code in
   `tools/train/`, weights versioned in `models/`. No third-party pretrained weights.
   Inference is C we wrote.
3. **The device works with the network unplugged.** Full stop.
4. **Systems core is C17**, `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`, no VLAs, `goto`-cleanup for
   multi-resource functions. Every allocation checked. Every syscall error path handled
   *and logged*.
5. **Python lives only in `tools/` and `ui/`.** No graded mechanism may hide there.
6. **Every daemon is supervisable:** clean exit codes, no orphaned fds across restart,
   heartbeat within 60 s of start, survives `kill -9` of any sibling.
7. **Replayed or synthesized data is labeled as such EVERYWHERE** — every record carries
   `src=live|replay|synth`. Integrity boundary, not a style choice.
8. **Never weaken, skip, or delete a test to make the suite pass.** If a test is wrong,
   say so and fix it deliberately, in its own commit, with the reason.

---

## 3. What we are building (the one-paragraph version)

A Raspberry Pi riding in a daily-driven car. A USB OBD2 adapter in the car's OBD2 port
gives it the car's own sensors (D-015); the car's USB-C port powers it — nothing is cut or
spliced (D-011). Through standard Mode 01 requests (D-012) it reads oil temperature,
coolant temp, MAP, O2 / fuel trims, RPM and load, and builds a statistical model of what
normal looks like *for this car, at this operating point*. It then reports deviations
that a mileage sticker and a check-engine light both miss. The owner reads it from their
phone over the device's own Wi-Fi — read-only, no internet (D-013); `obdctl` stays the
exact interface. A single warning light on the box blinks while it is on duty and
changes pattern when something needs attention (D-014).

**The user:** a named owner of a specific car who wants maintenance driven by measured
condition instead of a generic interval. Testbed: **Lance's 2015 Honda CR-V EX-L**, the
only one (D-016). Its sticker and its Maintenance Minder both *estimate* from how far and
how hard it has been driven; the device *measures* the engine's condition (D-007).

**The claim we defend:** *"detects the three faults we can induce on this vehicle, with
these measured error rates."* Not "predicts failure." (handout §5)

---

## 4. Mechanism commitments

We need two. We commit to **D** (append-only crash-consistent storage — power is cut at
every key-off) and **E** (multi-process with a supervisor), and measure both. **B**
(interrupt-driven input vs polling) and **F** (high-rate no-drop ring) come back only if a
Pi-side sensor is added (board item `pisensor`): Mode 01 through a USB adapter is too slow,
and has no interrupt of ours, to justify either. **A**, **C** and raw CAN are stretch only.
Full rationale: `docs/DECISIONS.md` §B.1 (D-017).

---

## 5. The intelligence

All of it ours. Operating-point binning → per-bin baselines → Mahalanobis residuals →
Theil–Sen trends → our classifier → state machine with hysteresis. Rationale and the
standing "threshold test" rule: `docs/DECISIONS.md` §D.

---

## 6. Ownership map

| Owner | Subsystems |
|---|---|
| **Camden** | `src/obd/`, `src/ipc/` |
| **Lance** | `src/store/`, `src/analysis/`, `tools/train/`, **`electricalDrawing/`** |
| **Shared** | `src/supervisor/`, `src/interface/`, `src/common/`, `Makefile`, docs |

Ownership means first authorship and answerability at the defense, not exclusivity.

---

# 7. Git and pull-request law

**This section is not advisory.** Our process grade is computed from transcripts
corroborated against commits; the git history is itself a graded deliverable; and neither
partner will break down a thousand-line diff to review it. A commit small enough to review
in ninety seconds is a commit that actually gets reviewed.

## 7.1 The five absolutes

Claude may **never**, under any instruction short of an explicit human override in the
current session:

1. **Commit to `main`.** Every change reaches `main` through a pull request.
2. **Merge, approve, or close a pull request.** Only a human merges. Ever.
3. **`push --force`, force-with-lease, rebase a pushed branch, amend a pushed commit, or
   `reset --hard` anything that has been pushed.** History that reviewers have read is
   immutable.
4. **`git add -A`, `git add .`, or `git commit -a`.** Stage explicit paths, always. An
   unintended file in a diff destroys a reviewer's trust in the whole PR.
5. **Commit a file whose full current contents were not read this session.** No blind
   edits to code you have not looked at.

Violating any of these is a stop-work event: say so, and do not attempt a workaround.

## 7.2 Branches

- `main` is protected, always green, and never committed to directly.
- **One branch per unit of work.** Naming: `<owner>/<milestone>/<slug>`
  — `camden/m3/obd-reader`, `lance/m3/store-recovery`, `camden/m2/design-doc`.
- **A branch has exactly one purpose.** If you discover unrelated work mid-branch, you do
  not fold it in. Note it, finish the branch, open a separate one.
- Branch lifetime: one session's work, three days maximum. A long-lived branch is a
  review you will never do.
- Branch from current `main`, freshly pulled. Never branch from another open branch
  without saying so in the PR.

## 7.3 Commit granularity — one commit, one responsibility

**There is no line-count limit.** A commit is sized by *what it is responsible for*, not by
how big the diff happens to be. A 200-line rewrite of a single function is **one** commit;
splitting it would force the reviewer to hold half a function in their head across two
reviews, which is worse than the problem it solves. Twenty lines spread across five
unrelated concerns is **five** commits, even though it is small.

**The test that decides it, every time:**

> Can the reviewer evaluate this as a **single yes-or-no decision**?

If approving requires accepting one part while objecting to another, it is more than one
commit. If rejecting any part means rejecting the whole thing anyway, it is one commit —
leave it alone.

**The one-sentence test, restated.** State the commit's responsibility in one sentence
without using "and". If you can, it is one commit no matter how many lines it took. If you
cannot, split along the "and".

### For code

The unit is **one behavior, one function, or one design principle applied.**

- Tests ship **in the same commit** as the behavior they test. Same responsibility.
- A refactor is its own responsibility — never folded into a feature.
- Formatting, renames, and file moves are **separate commits, labeled as such**, so the
  reviewer skims them at speed instead of hunting for logic buried in noise.
- Two subsystems means two commits, always, regardless of size.
- **Every commit builds and passes tests on its own.** This is the one hard rule in this
  section — it is what makes the history bisectable and each commit reviewable in isolation.

**Size as a smell, not a limit.** Past roughly 400 changed lines, stop and re-apply the
one-sentence test — large diffs *often* contain a smuggled second responsibility. If it
survives the test, commit it as one unit and **say in the `WHY` why it is indivisible.**
Then the reviewer knows the size was considered rather than accidental.

### For documentation, Markdown, and data files

The unit is **one resolved question or one decision** — not one file, not one section.

- Closing one open question that touches a line in six tables across three files is **one
  commit.** Splitting it is actively harmful: the reviewer can no longer see that the
  change was applied *consistently*, which is the only thing worth checking.
- A doc commit's diff is often wide and shallow. That is expected and correct.
- Never mix a **content** change with a **reflow/reformat** of the same file — the content
  change disappears into whitespace noise. Reformat separately, or not at all.
- Never mix filling in a TODO with restructuring the section around it.
- Never mix a decision's *record* with its *implementation* across files in a way that
  hides one inside the other — but **do** keep a decision and the code that enacts it
  together when they are genuinely one change (see §7.7).

**The check:** `git show <commit>` should answer exactly one question a human asked. If it
answers two, split. If it answers half of one, you committed too early.

## 7.4 Commit message format

```
M<n> <area>: <imperative summary, ≤ 72 chars>

WHAT:   One sentence. What changed, mechanically.
WHY:    1–3 sentences. The reason, in terms of a requirement, a decision ID,
        or a measurement. Never "to improve things."
REVIEW: What the reviewer should check hardest, and what I am least sure about.
VERIFY: The exact commands run and their result.
```

`<area>` is one of: `obd`, `ipc`, `store`, `analysis`, `supervisor`,
`interface`, `common`, `build`, `tests`, `tools`, `soak`, `docs`.

Real example:

```
M3 ipc: refuse push on full ring instead of overwriting

WHAT:   ring_push now returns false and increments an overrun counter when
        head - tail == RING_CAPACITY, rather than wrapping over slot[tail].
WHY:    DECISIONS.md B.3 — silent overwrite is the exact failure mechanism F
        exists to prevent; a gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis.
REVIEW: The memory ordering on the tail load. I used acquire so the producer
        cannot see a stale tail and wrongly declare the ring full; I am least
        sure whether relaxed would be sufficient here.
VERIFY: make && make test && make asan — all green, test_ring 3/3.
```

**Banned messages**, non-negotiable: `wip`, `fix`, `fixes`, `updates`, `misc`, `cleanup`,
`changes`, `more work`, `address feedback`, or any message that does not say what changed.

## 7.5 Pull requests

- **One PR = one reviewable claim.** Title matches the lead commit: `M<n> <area>: <what>`.
- **A PR is sized by its claim, not its diff.** If the title needs "and", split it. If a
  reviewer would have to approve part and object to part, split it. A PR that implements
  one coherent thing is the right size even when that thing was large — but say so in the
  body, and lay out the commit-by-commit list so the reviewer has a path through it.
- **Past ~10 commits or ~600 changed lines, re-apply the test rather than obey a number.**
  Most PRs that big contain two claims; the ones that genuinely do not are fine.
- **Open the PR as a draft at the first commit**, not at the end — so the partner can watch
  it grow and object early instead of at the finish line.
- A PR touching the **other partner's** owned area is titled `[cross]` and needs that
  partner's review specifically, not either partner's.
- The description uses `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md`, **every section filled**. A PR
  with an unfilled section is not ready for review, and Claude should not mark it ready.
- The description must contain **verbatim pasted output** of `make`, `make test`, and
  `make asan`. Not a claim that they passed. The output.
- The description must name the decision IDs the PR touches, and must contain a
  **"What I am least sure about"** paragraph that is not empty. If everything is certain,
  you have not thought hard enough about the diff.
- If a PR needs a diagram, an annotated log excerpt, or a timing capture to be
  understandable — put it in the PR body. Making the reviewer reconstruct context is how
  reviews stop happening.

## 7.6 The merge gate

**If the reviewer does not understand a line, the pull request does not merge.**

The remedy is never "trust it." The remedy is, in order of preference:

1. Claude explains it in a PR comment, in plain language, tied to the requirement.
2. The commit is split further, so each piece is obvious on its own.
3. The code is rewritten more simply, even at a cost in elegance or a few instructions.

A reviewer must be able to answer these about **any line** in the diff before approving —
they are the demo-day question set, asked early:

- What wakes this? What is it waiting on?
- What happens to this file descriptor / this allocation when the child dies?
- What is the error path, and what does it log?
- Why can't this drop, duplicate, or reorder a sample?
- Which requirement or decision made it this way rather than the obvious alternative?

Neither partner approves a PR they could not defend at the keyboard, alone, on demo day.
**Approving code you do not understand is the only unrecoverable mistake in this
workflow** — it is 20 individual points, and the defense will find it.

## 7.7 Session start and session end

**Start of session:**
1. Read `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/milestones.md`, `docs/DECISIONS.md`.
2. `python tools/board_sync.py --status` — pick work from **Ready**, nowhere else.
3. State whose session this is.
4. `git status` clean, `git pull` on `main`, create the branch.

**End of session — mandatory, every time:**
1. Nothing uncommitted. No stray files.
2. PR opened or updated, template filled, build/test/asan output pasted.
3. **Every decision made without a human present is appended to `docs/DECISIONS.md` as
   ⚠️ UNREVIEWED and listed in the Review Queue — in the same commit that implements it,
   never a later one.**
4. Print a session summary: branch name, each commit as one line, PR link, decisions added,
   and what specifically needs human review.

**Claude never marks a decision reviewed or LOCKED.** Only Camden or Lance does, by editing
the `Reviewed` field, in a commit authored by that human.

## 7.8 When to stop instead of commit

Stop and emit a structured blocker — the decision, the options, the cost of each, your
recommendation — rather than proceeding, when:

- the change carries two responsibilities and cannot be cleanly separated (§7.3)
- it requires a decision not already in `docs/DECISIONS.md`
- it would touch the other partner's owned area by more than a line
- it would weaken, skip, or delete a test
- `make`, `make test`, or `make asan` is not green
- you would have to guess at hardware behavior without evidence (see §8)

## 7.9 Volume and distribution

≥ 40 meaningful commits across the semester, **both partners well represented**. A history
where one partner authored under a quarter of the substantive commits is probed hard at the
individual defense. A pair of "final submission" commits is an automatic process-grade of
zero **for both partners**.

Commit *as you go*, inside the session. A session that produces one commit at the end has
already lost the granularity this section exists to protect.

## 7.10 Repository settings (humans, once)

On GitHub, set on `main`: require a pull request before merging · require 1 approval ·
dismiss stale approvals on new commits · require conversation resolution · block force
pushes · block deletions. Enable **squash-merge only if** the squash message is rewritten
to be meaningful — otherwise prefer merge commits, since our granular history *is* the
deliverable and squashing destroys it.

## 7.11 Issues and the project board — where work and questions live

**GitHub Issues replace the blockers list.** Anything that needs a human — a question, a
decision, a measurement only one of us can take, a part that must be ordered — is an
**issue**, not a paragraph buried in a doc or a session summary nobody re-reads.

`docs/DECISIONS.md` keeps only what has been **decided** (plus the review queue).
Everything still open lives on the board, where it has an owner, a milestone, and a
visible position in the queue.

### The board is generated, not hand-maintained

**`docs/board.toml` is the source of truth. GitHub is derived from it.**
`tools/board_sync.py` reconciles the two. Full contract in `docs/BOARD.md`; the part that
binds this section:

> **Never create, retitle, relabel, re-milestone or re-assign an issue with `gh` or in
> the web UI.** Edit the `[[item]]` and re-run sync. An issue created by hand is invisible
> to the manifest, drifts immediately, and is reported forever as unmanaged.

What you *may* do directly on GitHub: **comment**, **answer**, and **close**. Those are the
human parts, and sync respects all three — it never reopens what a human closed, and it
reports any issue closed on GitHub that `board.toml` still thinks is open, so the manifest
gets caught up in the next commit.

### Issue types

| Label | Meaning | Who closes it |
|---|---|---|
| `question` | Needs human judgment or knowledge Claude does not have | **Human only** |
| `decision` | A design choice that must be made before work proceeds | **Human only** |
| `task` | Work to be done; may be Claude's or a human's | PR merge, or owner |
| `bug` | Something is wrong | PR merge |
| `hardware` | Physical world: order it, wire it, measure it, drive it | **Human only** |
| `blocked` | Waiting on a dependency (applied and removed by sync) | n/a |

`board_sync.py` refuses to close a `question`, `decision` or `hardware` issue without the
explicit `--close-questions` flag, which is a human typing it. That is the enforcement, not
an honour system.

### Claude's standing instructions

- **When you would stop and emit a blocker (§7.8), add an `[[item]]` to `docs/board.toml`
  instead**, run sync, and continue with whatever else is unblocked. Link the issue number
  in the session summary.
- Title: `M<n> <area>: <what>` — same convention as commits.
- Body must state: what is blocked, what you already tried or know, the options with their
  costs, your recommendation, and **exactly what answer would unblock it**. A question a
  human can answer in one line beats a question that needs a meeting.
- Set `owner`. Unassigned issues are nobody's.
- Set `milestone` (`M0`–`M6`) so the board sorts by deadline.
- Give it a `slug` that will still make sense in Week 14. Slugs are permanent identity —
  **never rename or reuse one**; the slug→issue mapping in `docs/board.lock.json` is what
  survives between sessions.
- If the item exists because of a decision, set `decision = "D-###"`. Sync renders the link
  into the issue and warns if that ID is not in `docs/DECISIONS.md`.

### Dependencies — the gate

`blocked_by` in `board.toml` takes **slugs, never issue numbers**. Sync resolves them,
writes the `Blocked by: #12, #15` block into the body, and applies or removes the `blocked`
label as blockers open and close. It refuses to run on a dependency cycle or a dangling
slug, so a bad edit fails before it reaches GitHub.

The board column follows from that, automatically:

| Column | Means |
|---|---|
| **Backlog** | something it depends on is still open |
| **Ready** | nothing blocks it — this is the actionable list |
| **Blocked** | waiting on something that is *not* another item (a shipment, a reply) — set by hand |
| **In progress** / **In review** | set by hand while work is live |
| **Done** | the issue is closed |

**Do not start work on an issue that is not in Ready** — say so and pick up something that
is. Answering one question can move several cards into Ready on the next sync; that is the
board telling you what just became workable.

### Issue → branch → PR, as one chain

```sh
gh issue develop <n> --name camden/m3/obd-reader --checkout   # branch linked to issue
# ... commits per §7.3 ...
gh pr create --draft --title "M3 obd: Mode 01 reader on the adapter tty" --body-file <filled template>
```

The PR body must contain `Closes #<n>`. Merging then closes the issue; the next sync moves
the card to Done. **Every PR traces back to an issue**; if there is no issue, add the
`[[item]]` first — that is the record of *why* the work existed.

### Session end

Run `python tools/board_sync.py`. It is the only thing that moves cards, and it is cheap:
a run with nothing to do makes zero writes. **A board that lies is worse than no board**,
and the only way it can lie now is if you skipped this step.

CI enforces it: `.github/workflows/board.yml` runs `--check --no-board` on every push and
pull request and fails on drift, and `make test` validates `docs/board.toml` itself through
`tools/test_board.py`. So a forgotten sync is a red build, not a quiet lie.

### What this is worth at the defense

The board is not project-management theater. It is a timestamped record that the questions
were asked before the work, that a human answered them, and that the answer shaped the
code — which is precisely the process the transcripts are graded against, corroborated by
an independent system we did not write.

---

## 7.12 Hardware changes (KiCad)

The schematic lives in `electricalDrawing/` (KiCad 10, owned by Lance). KiCad files are
S-expression **text**, so hardware goes through the same branches, commits and pull requests
as the C — with two additions, both of which exist because a reviewer cannot read a diff of
coordinate tuples.

**Every PR touching `electricalDrawing/` must:**

1. **Include the regenerated schematic SVG** (`make hwdocs`, commit
   `docs/figures/electricalDrawing.svg`). A hardware PR without a picture is unreviewable,
   and §7.6 then blocks it — correctly.
2. **Show `make hwcheck` output in the body.** ERC violations are build failures, the same
   way `-Werror` findings are. Pasted output, not a claim.

**Commit granularity for schematics** follows the documentation rule in §7.3, not the code
rule: the unit is **one functional block or one resolved electrical question**. Wiring the
whole CAN block is one commit even if it moves fifty symbols. Renumbering references across
the sheet is a separate, labeled commit — never folded into a wiring change, for exactly the
reason formatting is never folded into logic.

**Never commit:** `.kicad_prl` (per-user state), `.history/`, autosave or backup files, or
anything under `make hwdocs`'s outputs except the schematic SVG. The `.gitignore` enforces
this.

**What Claude may not do here.** I cannot see the board. Symbol pin numbering, footprint
choice, placement, thermal, EMI and mechanical fit are all things I reason about blind, and
hand-writing `.kicad_pcb` geometry is forbidden — the coordinate math fails silently at fab.
I am useful for netlist review, datasheet cross-checks, design rules, BOM and export
scripting, and reading ERC JSON. **A measured voltage always beats my opinion**, and §8.4
applies with full force: no hardware conclusion from a verbal description or an unmeasured
module.

---

---

## 8. Workflow (non-git)

1. **Plan first.** Multi-file or algorithmic change: plan mode, wait for approval, no code
   until the plan is accepted.
2. **Explore before writing.** Read the existing code and the datasheet before proposing.
   Say what you read.
3. **Tests lead.** New behavior gets a test that fails first.
4. **Evidence over assertion — hardware clause (handout §10.2).** Never propose a hardware
   fix from a verbal description. Paste the artifact: `dmesg` verbatim, the raw adapter
   replies, the `vcgencmd get_throttled` reading, the timing histogram.
   Without evidence, your job is to say what to capture — not to guess.
5. **Adversarial review.** Every milestone's diff gets a fresh-context agent review *and* a
   human review by the partner who did not write it.
6. **Smallest diff that passes.** Do not refactor unrelated code. Do not "improve" things
   nobody asked about.
7. **Autonomous execution with declared blockers.** Run to completion on everything you
   can; stop with structured output at decisions that need human judgment.
8. **Credit discipline.** Minimal tool calls, no re-reads of files already in context, no
   re-derivation of settled results, batch independent work, smallest edits.

### Prompt quality bar (handout §10.4)

Useless: "make the sensor work." Effective: "`/dev/obd` opens and `ATZ` answers, but
`010C` returns `NO DATA` with the engine running. Here is our init sequence and the raw
replies [paste both]. Diff them against the ELM327 datasheet's protocol-selection steps and
identify the missing one; do not rewrite the reader."

---

## 9. Milestone hygiene — do not let this slip

**At every milestone M1–M5, each partner copies their raw `.jsonl` session files out of
`~/.claude/projects/` into `partners/<name>/transcripts/`.** Raw. Not summarized, not
exported, not retyped. Transcripts purge after 30 days by default and this project runs 15
weeks — losing Week-5 transcripts in Week 15 is a *foreseeable* loss and is not excused.

Each partner maintains `partners/<name>/PROMPTLOG.md` — 6–10 annotated episodes by M5,
including one revised plan, one rejected diff, one tool-output debugging loop with real
hardware evidence, and one review of the partner's work. **Write these as they happen.**

---

## 10. Deliverables checklist (handout §12)

- [ ] Source + `Makefile` + `README.md` that takes a TA from a clean Pi to running
- [ ] `docs/PROBLEM.md` (as revised), `docs/DESIGN.md` (as it ended + changelog of what M2 got
      wrong), `docs/EVALUATION.md`
- [ ] Raw unedited 48-hour soak logs including the injected fault
- [ ] `CLAUDE.md`, checked in, visibly evolving across milestones
- [ ] Per partner: `PROMPTLOG.md`, `REFLECTION.md`, raw `.jsonl` transcripts
- [ ] ≥ 40 meaningful commits spanning the milestones, both partners represented

---

## 11. Open blockers

**On the board, not in this file.** Open `question` and `decision` issues, in the Backlog
column of the `carwatch` project. `python tools/board_sync.py --status` lists them with
how long each has been open.
`docs/DECISIONS.md` records only what has been *decided*, plus the review queue. Nothing
open is tracked in two places, so nothing open can go stale in one of them.

---

*Last updated: M0 — §0, §7.11 and §11 rewritten when the board moved to
`docs/board.toml` + `tools/board_sync.py`. Both partners maintain this file.*

209	clamp (receive-only, a black box); powering the Pi from OBD2 pin 16 through our own buck
210	converter (live with the key off, and more hardware to build and defend).
211	
212	**Rule this imposes:** **the Pi must not brown out at crank.** The USB-C supply is rated
213	≥ 5.1 V / 3 A (Pi 4), and is proven by `vcgencmd get_throttled` after a cold start, not
214	by its label (`docs/hardware/wiring.md`).
215	
216	**Cost.**
217	- No recording while the key is off — nothing happens then worth recording, but the device
218	  also cannot run overnight in a parked car.
219	- **The OBD2 adapter itself draws from pin 16, which is live with the key off.** Its
220	  key-off current must be measured before it is left plugged in overnight.
221	- D-006 option (c), the parked-car soak, now requires a socket that stays live in
222	  accessory plus a battery tender.
223	- The product is "one box, two cables", not "one dongle".

225	## A.7 — Standard Mode 01 requests are the primary data path ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
226	`D-012` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
227	
228	*Revised 2026-09-21 by D-015, before any review: the CAN-level detail (arbitration IDs,
229	broadcast frames, a listen-only flag, the port-traffic check) went with the MCP2515.*
230	
231	**Decision.** The capture daemon gets its signals by sending **standard OBD2 Mode 01
232	requests** through the USB adapter (D-015) on a fixed, rate-limited, round-robin schedule,
233	one request outstanding at a time. Every timeout and every unanswered PID is logged.
234	
235	**Why.** D-011 makes this a plug-in device, and the thing that makes a plug-in device work
236	on a car it has never seen is the part of the protocol every car must speak: Mode 01 is
237	mandatory on US cars from model year 1996. *"Learns this car's normal"* is precisely what
238	lets one device serve different cars without per-model decode work: it never needs to
239	know what normal *is* ahead of time.
240	
241	**Sample-rate consequence.** Signals are round-robined, so each PID is sampled at
242	(request rate ÷ PID count) — on the order of 1 Hz each for a ~10 requests/s budget over
243	~8 PIDs. That is ample for what we diagnose (oil trend over weeks, warm-up over minutes,
244	fuel trim against load) and must be stated in `docs/DESIGN.md` §4. The request budget itself
245	is a design-doc number to justify, not a constant to pick.
246	
247	**Cost.** The device sends requests to the car's ECU. Kept safe by the rate limit, one
248	outstanding request, and only standard read-only Mode 01 requests — the same thing every
249	scan tool does.
250	
251	**Scope note.** "Works on any car" is the product's direction, not our claim. The claim is
252	still E.1: three faults, one car, measured error rates.

256	# B. Systems architecture and mechanisms
257	
258	## B.1 — Mechanism commitments: D and E; B and F only with a Pi-side sensor ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
259	`D-017` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
260	· **Supersedes:** D-002 (§G.3)
261	
262	The handout requires two, implemented by us and measured.
263	
264	| Mechanism | Status | Where |
265	|---|---|---|
266	| **D** — custom append-only storage, crash-consistent | **committed** | `src/store/` |
267	| **E** — multi-process with a supervisor | **committed** | `src/supervisor/`, `src/ipc/` |
268	| **B** — interrupt-driven input with a polling comparison | only if `pisensor` adds an MPU-6050 | capture path for that sensor |
269	| **F** — high-rate no-drop SPSC ring | only if `pisensor` adds an MPU-6050 | `src/ipc/ring.c` |
270	| **A**, **C**, raw CAN | stretch, after D and E are measured | — |
271	
272	**D.** *The defining constraint: power is cut mid-write every time the key turns off*
273	(D-011). We never get a clean shutdown. Measured by pulling power mid-write, repeatedly,
274	and proving recovery (`expcrash`).
275	
276	**E.** A recorder that dies silently has actively harmed its user, who believes it is on
277	duty. Any child may be `kill -9`'d; the system degrades, logs, recovers. Measured by killing
278	each child repeatedly and timing detection and recovery (`expkill`).
279	
280	**Why B and F left the OBD data path (D-015).** B needs an interrupt that *our* design
281	services. The USB adapter's interrupts belong to the kernel's USB-serial driver; our process
282	only blocks on a tty, and at ~10–20 replies/s a poll loop keeps up trivially — the
283	comparison would measure the tty layer, not a design of ours. F needs a *high-rate* stream;
284	~10–20 samples/s never stresses a ring, so "zero drops under contention" would be true and
285	meaningless.
286	
287	**What brings them back.** An MPU-6050 on the Pi's I2C, its `INT` pin on a GPIO: kHz
288	samples from a hardware FIFO give a real interrupt-vs-polling comparison (B) and a rate
289	that stresses the ring (F). That is board item `pisensor`, due at M2.
290	
291	**The ring stays regardless.** It is how capture hands samples to storage across the
292	process boundary E requires, and B.3 still binds it.
293	
294	**Risk.** D and E alone meet the floor exactly. If either measurement fails, nothing is in
295	reserve — which is why `pisensor` is on the critical path.
296	
297	## B.2 — Four processes, not one 🔒
298	`D-002` (corollary) · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
299	
300	`obdd`, `storaged`, `analyzed` and `supervisor` are separate processes with separate
301	address spaces, communicating over a shared-memory ring and Unix domain sockets.
302	
303	**Why.** Fault isolation is the product requirement, not an architectural preference: the
304	analysis engine is the most complex and least trustworthy component, and it must not be
305	able to take the capture path down with it. One process would be simpler and would fail
306	the thing the device exists to do.
307	
308	## B.3 — The ring refuses rather than overwrites 🔒
309	Decided M0 · **By:** Claude, from D-002 · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
310	
311	When the ring is full the producer returns failure and increments an overrun counter. It
312	does **not** overwrite the oldest unread slot.
313	
314	**Why.** Overwriting loses data silently, and silent loss is the exact failure mechanism F
315	exists to make impossible. A refusal is visible, countable, and reportable; an overwrite
316	looks like a quiet minute. Enforced by `tests/test_ring.c`.
317	
318	**Reviewer note.** This is a real trade: under sustained overload we drop *new* data
319	rather than *old*. If that is ever the wrong choice for a diagnostic, reopen this.
320	
321	## B.4 — The phone is a read-only window over the device's own Wi-Fi ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
322	`D-013` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
323	
324	**Decision.** The Pi runs its own Wi-Fi access point — WPA2, a per-device passphrase, **no

340	query verbs and exact semantics is more defensible, and far more extensible at the

346	- A network listener in the product. It binds only to the AP interface, is read-only, and

353	## B.5 — One warning light, driven by the supervisor ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
354	`D-014` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
355	
356	**Decision.** One LED on a GPIO (proposed GPIO17, header pin 11, through 330 Ω), written
357	**only by the supervisor**. Every state in which the device is working is a *blink
358	pattern*:
359	
360	| Light | Meaning | Priority |
361	|---|---|---|
362	| fast blink (~4 Hz) | **degraded** — a child is down, the adapter silent while the engine runs, storage failing, or undervoltage | highest |
363	| double-blink, pause | **a verdict has surfaced** (after D.3 hysteresis and dwell) — look at the phone | |
364	| slow blink (~1 Hz) | on duty, recording, nothing to report | lowest |
365	| **steady on or steady off** | **the device is not running.** Never a valid state. | — |
366	
367	**Why a light at all.** The 3 a.m. test: nobody is looking at a phone at the moment that
368	matters. It also makes "honest reporting through our own interface" (demo movement 1)
369	visible from across the room when a sensor is unplugged.
370	
371	**Why every live state blinks.** A GPIO keeps its last level after the process driving it
372	dies. If "verdict" were solid-on, a crashed supervisor would freeze the light into a false
373	alarm, or into a false all-clear if it froze off. With blink-only states, a stuck light of
374	either kind can only mean *not running*. This is mechanism E's principle — a recorder that dies
375	silently has harmed its user — applied to the one output a driver actually sees.
376	
377	**Why the supervisor, not `analyzed`.** The supervisor already knows every child's
378	liveness (mechanism E), so it can show "degraded" when `analyzed` itself has died; a light
379	owned by `analyzed` would show a stale verdict instead. Verdicts reach the supervisor over
380	the existing UDS. One writer, no GPIO contention.
381	
382	**Cost.** One more thing the supervisor does, and one more thing it must not block on: the
383	blink timer must never delay `waitpid` handling. Colour, brightness and placement are open
384	(M4 enclosure).

388	# C. Storage and data integrity
389	
390	## C.1 — Append-only, self-framing, CRC'd records 🔒
391	`D-002/D` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
392	
393	Records are never rewritten in place. Each carries a magic number for resynchronization
394	and a CRC32 over its whole body. Recovery scans from the last known-good offset, verifies
395	CRCs, truncates the torn tail, and logs exactly what was lost.
396	
397	**Why.** We are interrupted mid-write by design, several times a day. Rewriting in place
398	can destroy data that was previously correct; appending can only ever damage the last
399	record. The CRC is what makes a torn record *detectable* rather than merely wrong — and
400	wrong numbers you trust are more dangerous than missing numbers you know about.
401	
402	**Open sub-decision (M2, Lance):** fsync batch size and interval. There is no correct
403	value, only one justifiable from user requirements. Document the argument in `docs/DESIGN.md`
404	§4 before writing the code.
405	
406	## C.2 — Every record carries a provenance tag 🔒
407	Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
408	
409	Every record and every log line carries `src = live | replay | synth`. Present in the
410	format from day one, before any replay tooling exists.
411	
412	**Why.** Handout §5: replayed or synthesized data must be labeled everywhere it appears —
413	logs, report, demo. Making it a mandatory field rather than a convention means it is
414	structurally impossible to forget. Mislabeling synthesized data as live is the single
415	integrity failure this course is best equipped to detect, and the worst trade available
416	anywhere in it.

420	# D. Intelligence and analysis
421	
422	## D.1 — Self-trained model; training in Python, inference in C 🔒
423	`D-004` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden (confirmed with instructor) · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
424	
425	A locally-trained, self-authored model is permitted; hosted APIs and third-party
426	pretrained weights are not. Therefore: training in `tools/train/`, weights versioned under
427	`models/` with the training commit in the header, **inference in C in `src/analysis/`**, no
428	network at runtime.
429	
430	**Why inference in C.** First and most important for the grade: the runtime path sits
431	inside the supervised multi-process architecture, and a Python process there muddies the
432	boundary a grader must verify in sixty seconds. Second: it removes an interpreter, a
433	garbage collector and ~30 MB of RSS from a 48-hour memory-stability test we are graded on.
434	
435	**What the model is not doing.** The features are the intelligence — operating-point
436	binning, per-bin baselines, Mahalanobis residuals, Theil–Sen trends, all hand-written.
437	Delete the weights file and the system still produces residuals and trends; it loses only
438	the final labeling step. That separation is deliberate and it is the answer at the defense.
439	
440	## D.2 — Analysis pipeline shape 🔒
441	Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
442	
443	Operating-point binning (RPM × load × coolant temp) → per-bin running mean/variance →
444	multivariate residual (Mahalanobis) → robust trend (Theil–Sen) → classifier → state
445	machine with hysteresis and dwell.
446	
447	**Why binning comes first.** Comparing a cold idle to a warm cruise is a false-alarm
448	generator. Every comparison happens inside one bin, against genuinely comparable
449	conditions. This single step removes more false positives than anything else downstream.
450	
451	**Why multivariate.** The signal is the *correlation between sensors*, not any single
452	sensor's value — oil pressure is supposed to rise with RPM. A measure of anomaly that
453	already accounts for normal partnerships, and alarms only when a partnership breaks, is
454	what makes this something a threshold provably cannot do (handout §3.3).
455	
456	## D.3 — Hysteresis and dwell before any verdict surfaces 🔒
457	Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
458	
459	No verdict reaches the user until it has persisted. Trip and un-trip levels differ
460	deliberately.
461	
462	**Why.** A monitor that cries wolf twice gets unplugged, and an unplugged monitor is worse
463	than none because someone far away believes it is on duty. **False-positive rate is a
464	first-class metric in `docs/EVALUATION.md`, not an afterthought.**
465	
466	## D.4 — The threshold test, as a standing rule 🔒
467	Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
468	
469	Every diagnostic we ship must require at least two cooperating sensors to reach its
470	conclusion. If a single threshold on a single value could produce the verdict, it is not
471	intelligence and it does not count. **Write the reason down in `docs/DESIGN.md` when adding a
472	diagnostic** — this is checked at the defense.

592	## G.1 — (was A.1) CAN reaches the Pi via MCP2515 on SPI, not Bluetooth 🗑
593	`D-001` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
594	· **Superseded 2026-09-21 by D-015 (§A.1)** — raw CAN became a stretch goal.
595	
596	**Decision.** The Pi reads raw CAN frames through an MCP2515 + TJA1050 module on SPI0,
597	with the controller's `INT` line on a GPIO for edge-triggered receive. Not a Bluetooth
598	ELM327 dongle.
599	
600	**Why.** A Bluetooth ELM327 hands us parsed ASCII over a userspace socket at a few
601	samples per second. With no interrupt line, no SPI transaction and no bus-level timing,
602	mechanisms **A, B, C and F all become unavailable** — and the handout requires at least
603	two mechanisms implemented by us, below the application layer. The MCP2515 path keeps
604	the kernel boundary inside our repository, where it is graded. It is also better for the
605	user: raw bus access sees frames the ELM327 protocol never exposes, at the rate the ECU
606	publishes them rather than the rate a request/response dongle can poll.
607	
608	**Cost.** More wiring, a 3.3 V/5 V level question to get right, one-time decode work per
609	vehicle. Accepted.
610	
611	**What replaced it, and what that cost.** D-015 accepts the mechanism loss this entry
612	warned about, in exchange for hardware that works on day one; D-017 records which
613	mechanisms survive.

617	· **Superseded 2026-09-21 by D-016 (§A.2)** — the second vehicle was cut, as this entry
618	said it would be first.

620	**Decision.** Two daily-driven vehicles — Camden's Subaru Outback and Lance's Honda.
621	
622	**Why.** The product's thesis is that a generic maintenance interval is a generalization
623	and your car is not generic. One vehicle cannot demonstrate that; two with different duty
624	cycles can, and the comparison is the demo's strongest five seconds. Two also gives each
625	partner a vehicle they can instrument on their own schedule.

627	**Cost.** Roughly doubles decode and baseline-collection work, and the baseline window is
628	the one thing that cannot be compressed by working harder in Week 14. Mitigation: start
629	on standard Mode 01 PIDs only; manufacturer-specific frames are a stretch.
630

634	## G.3 — (was B.1) Mechanism commitments: B, D, E, F 🗑
635	`D-002` · Decided M0 · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
636	· **Superseded 2026-09-21 by D-017 (§B.1)** — with raw CAN a stretch goal (D-015), B and F
637	lost their data source.
638	
639	The handout requires two. We commit four and will measure all of them.
640	
641	**B — interrupt-driven input with a polling comparison.** `src/can/`. At 500 kbit/s a busy
642	bus delivers a frame roughly every 230 µs; the MCP2515's two receive buffers overflow in
643	milliseconds. A poll loop either burns a core or drops frames. Measured as event-latency
644	distribution and CPU, both ways, idle and loaded.
645	
646	**D — custom append-only storage, crash-consistent.** `src/store/`. *The defining
647	constraint: power is cut mid-write every time the key turns off.* We never get a clean
648	shutdown. Measured by pulling power mid-write, repeatedly, and proving recovery.
649	
650	**E — multi-process with a supervisor.** `src/supervisor/`, `src/ipc/`. A recorder that
651	dies silently has actively harmed its user, who believes it is on duty. Any child may be
652	`kill -9`'d; the system degrades, logs, recovers.
653	
654	**F — no-drop SPSC ring, sequence-accounted.** `src/ipc/ring.c`. Key-on produces a burst;
655	a gap in the record is a gap in the diagnosis. Measured as sustained rate with zero drops
656	under contention.
657	
658	**Stretch, M4+ only:** **A** (character driver for the MCP2515) and **C** (`SCHED_FIFO` on
659	the capture path). Do not start either until B, D, E and F are implemented *and measured*.
660	A half-finished kernel module is worth zero points and costs two weeks.
661	
662	---
663	
664	## Adding a decision
665	
666	Append it to the right category with the next free `D-###` for citation, and fill every
667	field. If Claude made it without a human present, it is ⚠️ **UNREVIEWED** and it goes in the
668	Review Queue at the top — **in the same commit that implements it**, never a later one.
669	
670	**Closing an open question.** When a human answers a `decision` or `question` issue, the
671	answer moves here as a 🔒 LOCKED entry citing the issue number, and the issue closes. One
672	commit does both — resolving one question is one responsibility, however many lines it
673	touches across this file (`CLAUDE.md` §7.3, documentation rules).
